questions.topic: Comprehension of whole or part of passage
questions.stem:
Attitudes towards the smoking of cigarettes and the consumption of alcohol may be used to illustrate typical African ethics. Apart from the fact that smoking has now been linked with lung cancer disease, the African moralist has always regarded smoking as an indication of moral degradation. A number of people have accepted the moralist idea on smoking. Some have refrained from smoking, and those who could influence others, such as parents and religious leaders, have also exerted their influence to prevent others from smoking. On the other hand, a good many people have remained indifferent to the moralist view and have continued to smoke. The same argument has been applied to the consumption of alcohol. The African moralist, basing his judgement on the behaviour of a few alcoholics, tends to regard the habit of taking alcohol as a sign of wretchedness. The moralist holds the view that anybody who forms the habit of consuming alcohol will never do well in life. While this may be true in respect of a few people in the society, the fear of the moralist has not been justified. However, the economist is primarily interested in the habit of smoking and the consumption of alcohol in so far as they give satisfaction to smokers and drinkers and so generate supply of and demand for tobacco and alcohol. The economist is interested in knowing how many packets of cigarettes are consumed and to what extent an increase or fall in consumption could affect production, that is, supply. Similarly, he is interested in how much beer is consumed and how the supply of beer will adjust to the demand for it. He examines the habits and the pressures which can lead to the readjustment of wants and the reallocation of resources to cover the wants.

Some moral principles associated with religion tend to lead on to economic problems. Followers of certain religions are expected not to consume pork, take alcohol or smoke tobacco. Devotees of some religious groups, on the other hand, can eat pork while others are expected to abstain from alcohol and smoking. Strict observance of these moral rules could cripple the breweries, the cigarette factories and some businesses. However, there seems to be a growing number of alcohol consumers and cigarette smokers – a development which should be of interest to the economist.

The positions maintained by the moralist and the economist can be described as being
questions.explanation: The moralist condemns smoking and drinking as degrading, while the economist values them for the demand and supply they generate - their positions differ.

Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
In spite of his humble beginning, Audu now throws his weight around.
options: Audu is arrogant despite his simple upbringing.
Despite his obvious poverty, Audu is a proud man.
His noble birth notwithstanding, Audu is a corrupt man.
From his poor background, Audu is now a rich man.
questions.explanation: To throw one's weight around is to behave arrogantly; 'humble beginning' means a simple upbringing.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
Ngozi has always considered her father to be an impassioned man.
options: Her father is a very lively man.
Her father is an emotional man.
Her father is a disciplined man.
Her father is a very strict man.
questions.explanation: Impassioned means filled with strong feeling, i.e. emotional.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
The elders rebuked Olu for taking issue with his principal.
options: Olu was cautioned for shouting at his principal.
Olu was scolded for acting in collusion with his principal.
Olu was reprimanded for arguing with his principal.
Olu was blamed for issuing a statement denying his principal.
questions.explanation: Key printed B; correct answer is C because to take issue with someone means to disagree or argue with them, and 'rebuked' means reprimanded.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
If he went to London, he would see the Queen.
options: When he goes to London, he will see the Queen.
He did not go to London and did not see the Queen.
He did not see the Queen when he went to London.
He would like to see the Queen when he goes to London.
questions.explanation: The past-tense conditional describes an unreal situation: he did not go, so he did not see the Queen.

questions.stem:

Only those who are [gullible] fall victim to his trickery.
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is D because gullible means easily deceived, and its opposite is astute (shrewd, hard to deceive); courteous means polite.

questions.stem:

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
Students could be [timid].
questions.explanation: Timid means shy and lacking courage; the opposite is bold.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The witness decided to [conceal] the evidence.
questions.explanation: To conceal is to hide; to divulge is to reveal.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The members of the congregation were [inspired] by the sermon.
questions.explanation: Inspired (uplifted, motivated) is opposed to disenchanted (disappointed, disillusioned).

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The labour leader's [recalcitrant] stance was applauded.
questions.explanation: Recalcitrant means stubbornly uncooperative; the opposite is flexible.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
A cool bath in a hot weather can be truly [invigorating].
questions.explanation: Invigorating means giving strength and energy; debilitating means weakening.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
I am [loath] to do the assignment.
questions.explanation: Loath means reluctant or unwilling; the opposite is willing.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
Toyin is married to [an impatient], self-centered man.
questions.explanation: An impatient person is intolerant of delay; the opposite is a tolerant (patient) person. Tolerable means bearable.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
[Gregarious] animals can be found in the zoo.
questions.explanation: Gregarious animals live in groups; the opposite is lonely/solitary.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The doctor examined the patient [painstakingly].
questions.explanation: Painstakingly means with great care; perfunctorily means carelessly, as a mere routine.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).

questions.stem:

questions.stem:

questions.stem:

questions.stem:

The boys knew that a storm was [imminent].
questions.explanation: Imminent means about to happen, i.e. impending.

Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The nurse was in favour of [voluntary euthanasia].
questions.explanation: Euthanasia is the deliberate painless ending of life to relieve suffering.

questions.stem:

The [cynics] feared that the nation's nascent democracy would fail.
questions.explanation: Cynics here are people who expect the worst, i.e. pessimists.

questions.stem:

The [essence] of governance is to seek the good and well-being of the majority of the people.

From what she said, one may [infer] that she does not like the course.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
He shared his room with a person whose behaviour was quite [nauseating].

Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The carpenter built a [commodious] wardrobe.
questions.explanation: Key printed A; correct answer is C because commodious means roomy, having plenty of space inside, i.e. spacious - not necessarily gigantic.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
Publishing as a business venture has become [a hot potato] in Nigeria.
questions.explanation: A hot potato is a difficult, unpleasant matter that people would rather avoid.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word(s) or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The man's story sounded [plausible] to his audience.
questions.explanation: Plausible means believable, i.e. credible (credulous describes a person who believes too easily).

Nowadays, many graduates are not well disposed to teaching, …

questions.stem:
Fill the gap with the most appropriate option.

questions.explanation: When 'woman' modifies a plural noun it also takes the plural form: women occupants.

questions.topic: Mood, tense, aspect, number, agreement/concord, degree and question tags
questions.stem:
Fill the gap with the most appropriate option.
It is often … that inflation … from too much money chasing very few goods.
questions.explanation: The passive 'It is often said' is needed, and singular 'inflation' takes 'results'.

questions.stem:
Fill the gap with the most appropriate option.
I have the … of meeting the President.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is privilege.

questions.stem:
Fill the gap with the most appropriate option.
My classmate, … I haven't seen for years, wrote to me last week.
questions.explanation: The relative pronoun is the object of 'seen' and refers to a person, so 'whom' is required (and 'that' cannot begin a non-defining clause).

questions.topic: Mood, tense, aspect, number, agreement/concord, degree and question tags
questions.stem:
Fill the gap with the most appropriate option.
Four weeks … enough for the police to conclude their investigation.
questions.explanation: A period of time treated as a single amount takes a singular verb: four weeks is enough.

questions.stem:
Fill the gap with the most appropriate option.
The doctor asked the patient what …
questions.explanation: In reported questions the word order is subject + verb and the tense is backshifted: what the problem was.

questions.stem:
Fill the gap with the most appropriate option.
He put … in a basket.
questions.explanation: Quantity comes before colour in the order of modifiers: a dozen white eggs.

questions.stem:
Fill the gap with the most appropriate option.
Idakwo ran … miss the train.
questions.explanation: 'Lest' is followed by 'should' or the subjunctive, not 'will' or 'may'.

questions.stem:
Fill the gap with the most appropriate option.
It was a free-for-all and the students were blamed for taking the law …
questions.explanation: The idiom is 'to take the law into one's own hands'.

questions.stem:
Fill the gap with the most appropriate option.
Ali plays … violin with remarkable skill.
questions.explanation: Musical instruments take the definite article after 'play': plays the violin.

questions.stem:
Fill the gap with the most appropriate option.
The candidate's charisma should be a … factor in winning the election.
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is B because the adjective needed before 'factor' is 'determining' (deciding); 'determinant' is chiefly a noun meaning a factor, so 'a determinant factor' is redundant.

questions.explanation: The th in teeth is the voiceless /θ/, as in thought; though has voiced /ð/.

questions.explanation: typist (TY-pist) and refuse as a noun (RE-fuse) are stressed on the first syllable; the verb rebel, superb and propose on the second.

questions.stem:
The word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the sentence relates.
My MOTHER served rice and fresh fish stew for dinner.
options: What kind of meal did your mother serve for dinner?
Did your mother serve rice and fresh fish stew for lunch?
What kind of stew did your mother serve for dinner?
Who served rice and fresh fish stew for dinner?
questions.explanation: Stress on MOTHER answers the question 'Who served…?'

questions.stem:
The word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the sentence relates.
The President SPOKE to the press.
options: Are these the pressmen that the President spoke to?
Did the President speak to the press?
Did the President write to the press?
questions.explanation: Stress on SPOKE contrasts the action: he spoke, rather than wrote, to the press.

questions.topic: Comprehension of words, phrases, clauses, sentences, figures of speech and idioms
questions.stem:
A Wolf, seeing a Lamb drinking from a river, wanted to find a pretext for devouring him. He stood higher up the stream and accused the lamb of muddying the water so that he could not drink. The lamb said that he drank only with the tip of his tongue, and that in any case he was standing lower down the river, and could not possibly disturb the water higher up. When this excuse failed him, the wolf said: 'Well, last year you insulted my father.' 'I wasn't even born then,' replied the lamb.

'You are good at finding answers,' said the wolf, 'but what do you mean by taking up so much of the path where I am walking?' The lamb, frightened at the wolf's angry tone and terrible aspect, told him, with all due submission, that he could not conceive how his walking on such a wide path could occasion him any inconvenience. 'What!' exclaimed the wolf, seemingly in great anger and indignation. 'You are as impudent as your father who seized me by the throat last year, and caused me to be kept in a cage for three months.'

'If you will believe me,' said the lamb, 'my parents are poor simple creatures who live entirely by green stuff; we are none of us hunters of your species.' 'Ah! I see it's no use talking to you,' said the wolf, drawing up close to him. 'It runs in the blood of your family to hate us wolves, and therefore, as we have come so conveniently together, I'll just pay off a few of your forefathers' scores before we part.' So saying, he leapt at the lamb from behind and garroted him.

The expression 'when this excuse failed him' suggests that the
options: wolf only made up the charges levelled against the lamb
lamb was more intelligent than the wolf
lamb was prepared for the charges levelled against him
wolf was uncertain of the charges levelled against the lamb
questions.explanation: The wolf was only looking for a pretext; when one excuse failed he simply invented another, showing the charges were made up.

questions.stem:
Choose the most appropriate option to fill gap 11 in the passage.

Capitalism is an economic system which is founded on the principle of free enterprise and the private ownership of the means of production and distribution. The ___(11)___ of capitalism claim that its essential characteristic is economic …(12)…. The producer is free to produce whatever goods he …(13)…, but the …(14)… is equally free to buy what he wants. There is a market mechanism under this system which brings the producer and consumer together and tends to equate the supplies of the one to the demands of the other, and …(15)… the whims and caprice of both. It is this same …(16)… mechanism which determines what prices the consumers pay to the producers, as well as what share of the total …(17)…, in cash or kind, goes to each of the four recognized …(18)… of production – land, labour, capital and organization. It is further claimed for this system that every person is capable of watching his or her own interest, and that whatever injustice is done by the …(19)… of the market mechanism, this mechanism tends to bring about a state of …(20)… between the producers and the consumers.
(Adapted from The Guardian, October 5, 2003, p. 10)
questions.explanation: Those who claim its virtues are its protagonists (supporters).

questions.topic: Comprehension of whole or part of passage
questions.stem:
One of the most potent elements in body language is eye behaviour. You shift your eyes, meet another person's gaze or fail to meet it and produce an effect out of all proportion to the trifling muscular effort you have made. When two people look searchingly into each other's eyes, emotions are heightened and the relationship tipped toward greater intimacy.

In normal conversation, each eye contact lasts only about a second before one or both individuals look away. Because the longer meeting of the eyes is rare, it is weighted with significance when it happens and can generate a special kind of human-to-human awareness. Most of the time, a lingering look is interpreted as a sign of attraction and this should be scrupulously avoided except in appropriate circumstances. A young woman once complained, 'That man makes me so uncomfortable, half the time when I glance at him he's already looking at me - and he keeps right on looking.'

Proper street behaviour requires a balance of attention and intention. You are supposed to look at a passer-by just enough to show that you are aware of his presence. If you look too little, you appear haughty or furtive, too much and you are inquisitive. Usually what happens is that people eye each other until they are about eight feet apart, at which point both cast down their eyes.

Much of eye behaviour is so subtle that we react to it only on the intuitive level. This has been demonstrated in elaborate experiments. Subjects sit and talk in the psychologist's laboratory, innocent of the fact that their eye behaviour is being observed from behind a one-way vision screen. In one fairly typical experiment, subjects were induced to cheat while performing a task, then were interviewed and observed. It was found that those who had cheated met the interviewer's eyes less often than was normal, an indication that 'shifty eyes' can actually be a tip-off to an attempt to deceive.

However, none of the facts of eye behaviour are cut and dried, for there are variations between individuals. People use their eyes differently and spend different amounts of time looking at others. Besides, no pattern of eye behaviour is precisely predictable in any normal conversation.

The young woman in the passage was uncomfortable because
options: the man appeared to be showing interest in her by his prolonged eye contact
the man's short and sharp gazes would tip the relationship toward greater intimacy
strangers who made the man's type of eye contact were likely to be dangerous
she was allergic to eye contact
questions.explanation: A lingering look is interpreted as a sign of attraction, and the man kept on looking at her.

Most of the time, a lingering look is interpreted as a sign of attraction and this should be scrupulously avoided except in appropriate circumstances. A young woman once complained, 'That man makes me so uncomfortable, half the time when I glance at him he's already looking at me - and he keeps right on looking.'

Proper street behaviour requires a balance of attention and intention. You are supposed to look at a passer-by just enough to show that you are aware of his presence. If you look too little, you appear haughty or furtive, too much and you are inquisitive. Usually what happens is that people eye each other until they are about eight feet apart, at which point both cast down their eyes.

Much of eye behaviour is so subtle that we react to it only on the intuitive level. This has been demonstrated in elaborate experiments. Subjects sit and talk in the psychologist's laboratory, innocent of the fact that their eye behaviour is being observed from behind a one-way vision screen. In one fairly typical experiment, subjects were induced to cheat while performing a task, then were interviewed and observed. It was found that those who had cheated met the interviewer's eyes less often than was normal, an indication that 'shifty eyes' can actually be a tip-off to an attempt to deceive.

However, none of the facts of eye behaviour are cut and dried, for there are variations between individuals. People use their eyes differently and spend different amounts of time looking at others. Besides, no pattern of eye behaviour is precisely predictable in any normal conversation.

lack of uniformity in eye behaviour and the variability of contact situation
that some subjects cheat during experiments, thus invalidating research findings
that research findings on eye contact have not been subjected to further empirical tests
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the facts are not 'cut and dried' because individuals vary and no pattern is precisely predictable.

questions.stem:
The Second World Black and African Festival of Arts and Culture (FESTAC) was staged in Nigeria in 1977. At the colloquium organised during the festival, various issues affecting the development of the black world, including the inability of most independent African nations to make a clean break with the language of colonialism, were discussed by seasoned intellectuals. It was resolved then that each African country should assign important functions to its major indigenous language in order to facilitate the selection of one of them to replace the colonial language at the national level. This, it was hoped, could bring about the much-needed unity and national integration. Besides, since the different European languages in use were considered to be unsuitable for the expression of African cultural values, African countries were urged to promote their cultures in their local languages.

As they put it, no language could effectively ex[…] in that language; therefore, a campaign should be mounted, as a matter of urgency, to give impetus to the promotion of African languages. The media in each country, it was suggested, should spearhead the quest for an indigenous national language by educating, motivating and mobilizing their government and people towards the selection of an appropriate local language. This, in itself, was a recognition that the media - a term usually applied in reference to all the important agencies of mass information and entertainment, like the press, the radio and the television - wield tremendous and immeasurable power through their ability to mobilize the people and modify their behaviour, particularly towards important national issues. Regrettably, the media in Nigeria are yet to take up such major roles that would facilitate the emergence of an indigenous national language in the country.

Which of the following is true according to the passage?
options: The sole purpose of FESTAC was to discuss the language problems of Africa and the black world.
The media in Africa can enforce indigenous national languages.
National unity and cohesion will be enhanced through an indigenous national language.
Colonial languages are to blame for all the problems of Africa.
questions.explanation: An indigenous national language, it was hoped, could bring about the much-needed unity and national integration.

Nigeria has been playing a [vital] role in the political and economic development of Africa.

One of the most difficult and confusing aspects of the English language is its spelling system. There is often ___(16)___ between the pronunciation of a word and its spelling. One cannot always tell how to spell a word …(17)… its pronunciation. In order to understand the peculiarity of the English spelling …(18)…, it is good to know something about the history of the language. First, it is helpful to realize that English was originally spoken by people who could neither read nor write. While the …(19)… people spoke English, the literate upper classes spoke French and wrote in Latin. Later, when English became a …(20)… language, there was no system for spelling its words. Moreover, the first writers of English were French-speaking …(21)… who knew English only slightly; therefore, they carried many French spelling …(22)… into English. In addition, these first writers of English, who were used to writing in Latin, often …(23)… letters into words even when they were not pronounced because the …(24)… word in Latin was spelled that way. Finally, the confusion increased when the …(25)… of certain words changed while the spelling remained the same.
questions.explanation: The point is that spelling and pronunciation often do not match - a discrepancy.

questions.topic: Comprehension of whole or part of passage
questions.stem:
It is of no more use to give advice to the idle than to pour water into a sieve, but it strikes me that lazy people ought to have a large looking glass hung up where they are bound to see themselves in it. For sure, if their eyes are at all like mine, they will never bear to look at themselves long or often. The ugliest sight in the world is one of those thorough-bred loafers, who would hardly hold up his basin if it were to rain with porridge: and for certain, would never hold up a bigger pot than he wanted to fill for himself. Perhaps, if the shower should turn to beer, he might wake himself up a bit; but he will make up for it afterwards, since as a slothful man, he folds his hands in sleep and hates to get up even for his meals. Men like him ought to be treated with like the drone which the bees drive out of their hives for inactivity overdependence.

Every man ought to have patience and pity for poverty; but for laziness, a long whip might be better. This would be a healthy treatment for all sluggards, but there is no chance of some of them getting their full dose of this medicine, for they were born with silver spoons in their mouths, and like spoons will scarce stir their own tea unless somebody lends them a hand. They are like the proverbial dogs that leaned his head against the wall to bark and, like lazy sheep, it is too much trouble for them to carry their own wool. If they could see themselves, it might by chance do them a world of good; but perhaps it would be too much trouble for them to open their eyes even if the glass were hung for them.

If I seem to hit hard at the sluggards, it is because I know they can bear it, for if they were seed on the threshing floor, you will thresh many days to get them out of the straw, for laziness is in their bones, and will show itself in their idle flesh, no matter what you do with them.

One conclusion that can be drawn from the opening paragraph is that
options: it a waste of time to advise lazy man because he will always use a sieve to sift the advice
lazy people are thorough-bred loafers who cannot even eat their porridge
though lazy people have ugly faces, they like to see themselves in the mirror
lazy people work only to satisfy their own immediate needs
questions.explanation: The loafer "would never hold up a bigger pot than he wanted to fill for himself", i.e. he works only for his own immediate needs.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
The court brought out the fact that the elections were not free and fair.
options: The court said that the elections were not rigged
The court explained that the elections were not marred
The court made it clear that the elections were not flawless
The court saw that the elections were properly conducted
questions.explanation: Elections that were not free and fair were not flawless.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
The computer operator was sacked for incompetence
options: The computer operator was sacked for his foolishness
The computer operator was sacked for his laziness
The computer operator was sacked for lack of skill
The computer operator was sacked for lateness
questions.explanation: Incompetence is lack of the necessary skill.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
He was a member of the think tank of the previous administration
options: As an expert, he criticized government
He was an expert who gave advice to government
He was an expert that government did not listen to
As an expert government must have taken to his advice
questions.explanation: A think tank is a group of experts that advises government.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
In spite of various criticisms, Bala sticks to his guns.
options: Bala always goes out with his guns, ready to kill
People do not like Bala because he is violent
Bala is criticized because of his bad behaviour towards people
Bala adheres to his beliefs even when others do not agree with him
questions.explanation: To "stick to one's guns" is to keep to one's beliefs despite opposition.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
Chike plays to the gallery whenever he meets a group of people.
options: Chike plays well with people at the gallery
Chike likes to play with people
Chike shows distrust and hatred to people
questions.explanation: To "play to the gallery" is to act in a way meant to win cheap popularity.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
He kept a stiff upper lip over the accident.
options: He sustained injury on his upper lip
He endured the misfortune with courage
He could not talk because of the accident
His friends deserted him because of the accident
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is B because keeping "a stiff upper lip" means bearing misfortune bravely without showing emotion.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
She wriggled out of her wedding gown.
options: She could not take off her gown herself so she was assisted
Her dress got torn because of the snake-like pattern
No one could have imagined that her dress was so tight
It took her some time to remove her close-fitting dress
questions.explanation: To "wriggle out of" a close-fitting dress is to get out of it with twisting effort, slowly.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
The group had been made a scape goat during the event.
options: Members of the group had been punished for a sin that they did not commit
Members of the group had been blamed for a sin that they committed
The group had been punished so that no one would commit the sin again
The group had been blamed merely to serve as a deterrent to others
questions.explanation: Key printed D; correct answer is A because a scapegoat is one made to bear the blame or punishment for others' wrongdoing.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
Sola is [apathetic] about his work.
questions.explanation: "Apathetic" means lacking interest; the opposite is enthusiastic.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The members of the family had a [hasty] breakfast before starting out on their journey.
questions.explanation: A "hasty" breakfast is hurried; the opposite is leisurely.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The [poverty] level among the masses is unbearable.
questions.explanation: The opposite of poverty is affluence (wealth).

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The chairman was accused of implementing policies that favoured the [elite].
questions.explanation: The elite are the privileged few; the opposite is the oppressed.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The manager was impressed by the man's [eagerness].
questions.explanation: Key printed D; correct answer is B because eagerness is keen interest; the opposite is indifference.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The lecturer's [obscure] publications counted against him during the promotion exercise.
questions.explanation: "Obscure" publications are little known; the opposite is widespread.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The man found his wife physically [repellant].
questions.explanation: "Repellant" (repellent) means repulsive; the opposite is attractive.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
As an [absolute ruler], Adayi brooks no opposition from his subordinates.
questions.explanation: An absolute ruler is a dictator; the opposite is a magnanimous democrat.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The response to the advertisement has been [phenomenal].
questions.explanation: "Phenomenal" means remarkably great; the opposite is unimpressive.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
Bola's parents went through an [acrimonious] divorce.
questions.explanation: An "acrimonious" divorce is bitter; the opposite is peaceful.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
Iliya's account of the incident is [appalling].
questions.explanation: "Appalling" means shocking/horrifying; the opposite is fascinating.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
She [encapsulated] her view of the nature of life in a poem.
questions.explanation: To "encapsulate" is to sum up briefly; the opposite is to expatiate on (speak at length).

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
We were held [spellbound] by his eloquence.
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is A because held "spellbound" means enthralled; the opposite is unimpressed.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
We were at a loss to understand why Oli should [retract] his statement before the Judge.
questions.explanation: To "retract" a statement is to withdraw it.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The workers hope to appear before the [arbitration] panel to resolve the lingering dispute.
questions.explanation: An arbitration panel settles disputes — it is reconciliatory.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
He went to the polls in defiance of sound advice and recorded an [abysmal] performance.
questions.explanation: "Abysmal" means extremely bad — disappointingly bad.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
He was not able to [withstand] the attack from his immediate family.
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is D because to "withstand" an attack is to resist it.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
Your effort to bring peace between us is futile because you are [biased].
questions.explanation: "Biased" means prejudiced.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).

questions.explanation: A door "ajar" is slightly open, i.e. half-closed — not locked, sealed or permanently open.

questions.stem:

questions.explanation: An "exacting" task is demanding.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).

questions.explanation: Remonstrances are forceful protests.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).

questions.explanation: A "throng" is a large crowd.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The man's wife has her [misgivings] about him.
questions.explanation: Misgivings are doubts or distrust.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
Violent crime is only one of the [maladies] afflicting modern society

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
Ade has an [aquiline] nose.
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is A because an aquiline nose is hooked like an eagle's beak — large and curved.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
Everyone was talking about the [camaraderie] in the club.
questions.explanation: Camaraderie is friendship and companionship.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
'You're [impossible],' she said to me.
questions.explanation: Calling someone "impossible" means they are very unreasonable to deal with.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).

questions.explanation: A "sixth sense" is intuition.

Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).

questions.explanation: The idiom is "pay in instalments".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
The scholar examined ____ of the subject.
questions.explanation: A compound adjective before a noun is hyphenated and singular: "a three-part analysis".

Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).

questions.explanation: One "opts for" something, and the compound adjective is "out-of-court".

Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
She refrained ____ smoking.
questions.explanation: The verb "refrain" takes "from".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Birds whistle while bears ____.

questions.stem:

questions.stem:

questions.stem:
The word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates.
THEIR children speak better French than English.
options: Do their husbands speak better French than English?
What language do their children speak better than English?
Do their children speak better French than English?
Whose children speak better French than English?

They RAN to the playground.

Did they run from the playground?
questions.explanation: Stress on RAN contrasts running with another way of moving, e.g. walking.

The word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates.
Timi BOUGHT a new car.
options: Did Timi hire a new car?
Has Timi acquired a new car?
Does Timi have a new car?
questions.explanation: Stress on BOUGHT contrasts buying with another way of getting, e.g. hiring.

questions.topic: Comprehension of whole or part of passage
questions.stem:
There are many indicators with which to assess or measure corruption. One of them is the affluent living habit of the public official compared to his/her income. Corruption occurs when a public official expects to be induced to perform an act which that public official is ordinarily required to do by law. Corruption can slow down development. One of the most widely discussed consequences of corruption is the distortion of governmental expenditure. This often results in public money being wasted on white elephant projects, rather than people-oriented services such as health and education. As a result, more opportunities are presented for corrupt use or diversion of funds. Raising the ethical standards of governance can lead to many benefits especially for the economic, political and social development of a country. Fighting corruption and promoting governance is therefore crucial to developing an environment that facilitates the social, political and economic development of the people. However, while there are often general statements made about the effects of corruption on poverty and development, there is not an explicit recognition that corruption is more than just wealth misappropriation or abuse of power. Corruption impoverishes countries and deprives their citizens of good governance. It destabilizes economic system. When organized crime and other illegal activities flourish, basic public functions are eroded and the quality of life of the people is reduced. Bribery, for example is universally regarded as a crime, but it also reflects socioeconomic problems that require broad-based preventive measures and the involvement of the society at large.

Another implication of global measures against corruption is making government work better by improving the economy. Finally, redesigning political and regulatory structures will reduce corruption and other antisystem players that encourage corrupt practices.

From the passage, one of the consequences of corruption is that
options: it is beneficial to wealthy people who stole public wealth
it impedes the progress of a nation
people get what they want with so much money to spend
questions.explanation: The passage says "corruption can slow down development" — it impedes a nation's progress.

questions.topic: Comprehension of whole or part of passage
questions.stem:
Like a clock with the pendulum in full swing, the mind moves as fast as time. But we ought to mind our thoughts, for if they turn to be our enemies, they will be too many for us and will drag us down to ruin. But some people may say that they cannot help having bad thoughts even though they sting like vipers. That may be true, but the question is: do they hate them or not? We cannot keep thieves from looking in at our windows, but if we open our doors to them and receive them joyfully, we are as bad as they. We cannot help the birds flying over our heads; but we may keep them from building their nests in our hair. Vain thoughts will knock at the door but we must not open to them.

Though bad and evil thoughts rise in our hearts, they must not be allowed to reign. He who turns a morsel over and over in his mouth does so because he likes the flavour, and he who meditates upon evil, loves it, and is ripe to commit it. Think of the devil, and he will appear; turn your thoughts towards evil and your hands will soon follow. Snails leave their slime behind them, and so do vain thoughts. An arrow may fly through the air and leave no trace, but an evil thought always leaves a trail like a serpent.

Where there is much traffic of bad thinking, there will be much mire and dirt. Every wave of wicked thought adds something to the corruption which rots upon the shore of life. It is dreadful to think that a vile imagination, once indulged, gets the key of our minds, and gets in again very easily, whether or not we let it in, and what may follow, no one knows. Nurse evil on the lap of thought, and it will grow into a giant. Therefore, there is wisdom in watching every day the thoughts and imaginations of our hearts. Good thoughts are blessed guests and should be welcomed, well fed, and much sought after, but bad thoughts must fly out as swiftly as they moved in.

Which of the following statements represents the view expressed by the writer in the first paragraph?
options: Evil thoughts will eventually ruin the evil man
If we do not stop the pendulum of thoughts from swinging, our thoughts will soon become our enemies
Too many evil thoughts leave fatal consequences
It is possible to decide what controls our thoughts
questions.explanation: The first paragraph warns that thoughts that turn into enemies "will be too many for us and will drag us down to ruin".

But some people may say that they cannot help having bad thoughts even though they sting like vipers. That may be true, but the question is: do they hate them or not? We cannot keep thieves from looking in at our windows, but if we open our doors to them and receive them joyfully, we are as bad as they. We cannot help the birds flying over our heads; but we may keep them from building their nests in our hair. Vain thoughts will knock at the door but we must not open to them.

Though bad and evil thoughts rise in our hearts, they must not be allowed to reign. He who turns a morsel over and over in his mouth does so because he likes the flavour, and he who meditates upon evil, loves it, and is ripe to commit it. Think of the devil, and he will appear; turn your thoughts towards evil and your hands will soon follow. Snails leave their slime behind them, and so do vain thoughts. An arrow may fly through the air and leave no trace, but an evil thought always leaves a trail like a serpent.

Where there is much traffic of bad thinking, there will be much mire and dirt. Every wave of wicked thought adds something to the corruption which rots upon the shore of life. It is dreadful to think that a vile imagination, once indulged, gets the key of our minds, and gets in again very easily, whether or not we let it in, and what may follow, no one knows. Nurse evil on the lap of thought, and it will grow into a giant. Therefore, there is wisdom in watching every day the thoughts and imaginations of our hearts. Good thoughts are blessed guests and should be welcomed, well fed, and much sought after, but bad thoughts must fly out as swiftly as they moved in.

Which of the following statements summarizes the argument of the last paragraph?
options: Heavy traffic on a miry and dirty road may lead to evil thoughts
The more evil we think, the more vile we are likely to become
Evil people should not be welcomed as guests in our homes the same way as we welcome good people
Evil thoughts control the key to the human heart and no one can keep them out
questions.explanation: Every wave of wicked thought adds to the corruption, and evil nursed in thought "will grow into a giant".

questions.stem:
In 1962, a team of scientists produced a special radio station that had a range of fifteen miles. Even though communication was being accomplished in space at a range of more than a million times this distance, the new radio station caused more excitement among scientists. The reason: its power supply was a 'battery' made of bacteria. For the first time, practical amounts of electricity were being produced by a form of life and put to use.

Called the 'bio cell', the new power supply had a liquid fuel containing tiny forms of life that changed the fuel directly into electric energy. This was far more than an interesting experiment. The bio cell is being developed as a producer of electricity for radios, for signals to guide ships, for lighting and for other uses. Though the working bio cell is only a few years old, some scientists feel that it will one day produce power as cheaply as is now being done by other methods, and that the bio cell will use materials that would otherwise be considered a waste. Early bio cells were powered with sugar, but a wide range of fuels can be used. Work is being done using sea water to feed the bacteria.

Electricity from living cells is no new idea. Man experienced the strange 'shock' produced by some fish even before electricity was really discovered. Then in time, there were other discoveries. Benjamin Franklin found that lightning in the sky was electricity. Luigi Galvani found some electricity in the muscles and nerves of animals. But the African catfish produces far more electricity than most other living creatures. And another fish, the electric eel, is well named, for it has an even greater electric charge. Research workers also discovered that even humans produce small amounts of electricity in their bodies. Our hearts produce a very small amount that can be measured, so do our brains. The bio cell is completely new in the field of power production and, as yet, no mass-produced models have begun to replace the older types of batteries. It might be wondered, then, what the excitement is all about.

A suitable title for the passage is
questions.explanation: The passage is about electricity produced by living things, from the bacterial bio cell to fish and the human body.

The IPCC reports that the world has warmed by an average of 0.76°C since pre-industrial times. The rising global …(23)… for energy and the adverse changes in the climate put the earth and its inhabitants in a catch-22 situation.

Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word(s).
Mrs. Asio wanted her sister to stop being so [detached].
questions.explanation: Detached means aloof and emotionally uninvolved, i.e. indifferent.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word(s).
Lantana [dwelt] in a ruined cottage on the hillside.
questions.explanation: Dwelt (past of dwell) means lived.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word(s).
The mistake brought the show to an [ignominious] end.
questions.explanation: Ignominious means shameful or disgraceful.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word(s).
He [compliments] me on my way of doing things.
questions.explanation: To compliment someone is to praise them; "complements" is a different word (completes).

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word(s).
The girl is angry with her friend who had [ensnared] her into this relationship.
questions.explanation: To ensnare is to trap someone, especially by trickery.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word(s).
Their new house was roofed with [corrugated] sheets.
questions.explanation: Corrugated sheets are shaped into folds or ridges.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word(s).
The stockbroker said it was an [astute] move to sell the shares then.
questions.explanation: Astute means shrewd and clever.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word(s).
The principal described Oche as the most [tactful] person he had ever worked with.
questions.explanation: Key printed D; correct answer is B because tactful means handling people sensitively without giving offence, i.e. discreet; innovative is unrelated.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word(s).
The old woman is suffering from [dementia].
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is B because dementia is the decline of mental faculties typical of old age, i.e. senility, not insanity (madness).

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word(s).
Some drugs have a [deleterious] effect on a child's development.
questions.explanation: Key printed A; correct answer is C because deleterious means harmful; debilitating specifically means weakening.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word(s).
Fila has always been described as [belligerent].
questions.explanation: Belligerent means aggressive and combative.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word(s).
Laraba saw a [forlorn] little figure sitting outside the class.
questions.explanation: Forlorn means sad, lonely and abandoned.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word(s).
The circular [supersedes] all previous correspondence on the matter.
questions.explanation: To supersede is to take the place of, i.e. displace.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word(s).
Her problem was [exacerbated] by the loss of her father.
questions.explanation: Exacerbated means made worse, i.e. aggravated.

questions.topic: Mood, tense, aspect, number, agreement/concord, degree and question tags
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
When his car tyre ......... on the way, he did not know what to do.
questions.explanation: Simple past "burst" (irregular: burst-burst-burst) matches "did not know"; "bursted" is wrong.

questions.topic: Mood, tense, aspect, number, agreement/concord, degree and question tags
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Lami's father ........ as a gardener when he was young, but now he is a driver.
questions.explanation: "Used to" + verb expresses a past habit or state that no longer exists.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
........ he switches on the light, the shadow disappears.
questions.explanation: "Whenever" introduces a clause of time meaning "every time".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
The policemen became suspicious as the hoodlums ...... in their office.
questions.explanation: Key printed B; correct answer is C because the intransitive phrasal verb is "ferret about" (search around), and the past tense is spelt "ferreted" with one t.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
It is important that you clear the refuse in front of your house every ........
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is "fortnight" (two weeks).

questions.topic: Mood, tense, aspect, number, agreement/concord, degree and question tags
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Suara needn't come with us, .......?
questions.explanation: With modal "needn't" the positive question tag repeats the modal: "need she?"

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Unoka .... the whole house to find his missing wristwatch.
questions.explanation: Key printed D; correct answer is B because to "scour" a place is to search it thoroughly; scouted means reconnoitred.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Ife asked me .......
options: what is it by my time
questions.explanation: In reported speech the question becomes statement order and the tense is backshifted after "asked": "what time it was".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
There are many ways to kill a rat, so we should be ..... in our approach to the task ahead of us.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is "eclectic" (drawing on many methods).

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Audu took these actions purely ...... his own career.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is "in furtherance of" (to advance).

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Here is Mr. Odumusu who teaches English ....... in our school.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is "pronunciation" (no "o" after the first "n", unlike "pronounce").

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Instead of ......., she lied.
questions.explanation: The preposition "of" takes a gerund, and the subject is already "she": "Instead of pleading, she lied."

questions.topic: Mood, tense, aspect, number, agreement/concord, degree and question tags
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Of the three girls, Uka is the ........
questions.explanation: Comparing three or more needs the superlative degree: "the naughtiest".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
I wonder how he will ...... being absent from school for a long time.
questions.explanation: To "make up (for)" is to compensate for something missed.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Please sit on the .......
questions.explanation: A carrier is the seat/rack at the back of a bicycle; "career" means profession.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
I want to ....... this chance to acquaint you with the latest development.
questions.explanation: "Seize" (take hold of) is spelt with "ei"; size and cease are different words.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Getting a well paid job nowadays is an ...... task.
questions.explanation: An uphill task is a very difficult one.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
The secretary has no right to ....... my affairs.
questions.explanation: One "meddles in" another person's affairs.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Bola studiously avoided ....... the questions.
questions.explanation: Studiously avoiding the questions means deliberately not answering them.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
The school authority dismissed him for ...... but I won't tell you about it yet.
questions.explanation: "Reason" is countable and needs an article; "a certain reason" means a particular reason not yet stated.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the underlined (shown in [brackets]) letter(s).
b[u]bble
questions.explanation: The "u" in bubble is /ʌ/, as in bumper /ˈbʌmpə/; bull has /ʊ/, gurgle /ɜː/, guy /aɪ/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the underlined (shown in [brackets]) letter(s).
w[ei]ght
questions.explanation: "ei" in weight is /eɪ/, as in whale /weɪl/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the underlined (shown in [brackets]) letter(s).
l[ea]ch
questions.explanation: "ea" in leach is /iː/, as in cedar /ˈsiːdə/; gear and cheer have /ɪə/, death /e/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the underlined (shown in [brackets]) letter(s).
men[t]ion
questions.explanation: The "t" in mention is /ʃ/, as "ch" in machine /məˈʃiːn/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the underlined (shown in [brackets]) letter(s).
presti[ge]
questions.explanation: "ge" in prestige is /ʒ/, as "s" in leisure /ˈleʒə/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the underlined (shown in [brackets]) letter(s).
[kn]ot
questions.explanation: "kn" in knot is /n/ (the k is silent), as in the only option beginning with /n/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that rhymes with the given word.
fuel
questions.explanation: Fuel /ˈfjuːəl/ rhymes with cruel /ˈkruːəl/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that rhymes with the given word.
match
questions.explanation: Match /mætʃ/ rhymes with batch /bætʃ/; watch has /ɒ/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that rhymes with the given word.
sheer
questions.explanation: Sheer /ʃɪə/ rhymes with ear /ɪə/.

questions.stem:
Choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. The stressed syllables are written in capital letters.
termination
questions.explanation: Termination /ˌtɜːmɪˈneɪʃn/ is stressed on the third syllable, -NA-.

questions.stem:
Choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. The stressed syllables are written in capital letters.
meditative
questions.explanation: Key printed B; correct answer is C because in British RP meditative is /ˈmedɪtətɪv/, stressed on the first syllable.

questions.stem:
Choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. The stressed syllables are written in capital letters.
suggestible
questions.explanation: Suggestible /səˈdʒestəbl/ is stressed on the second syllable, -GGES-.

questions.stem:
The word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates.
Uche LOVES Toyota cars.
options: What brand of car Uche love?
questions.explanation: Stress on LOVES contrasts the verb, answering whether Uche hates Toyota cars.

questions.stem:
The word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates.
The POLICE arrested the suspect.
options: Did the police placate the suspect?
Did the police arrest the suspect?
questions.explanation: Stress on POLICE identifies who did the arresting.

questions.stem:
The word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates.
Maiduguri is the CAPITAL of Borno State.
options: Is Maiduguri the capital of Plateau State?
Which State is Maiduguri the capital of?
Is Maiduguri a town in Borno State?
What is the capital of Borno State?
questions.explanation: Stress on CAPITAL contrasts it with being just "a town" in Borno State.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
The vice chancellor is riding the crest of the last quarter of his administration.
options: The vice chancellor enjoys the acknowledgment of the success of his administration
the vice chancellor does not enjoy the people's criticism of his administration
the vice chancellor hopes to overcome soon the poor comments on the administration
the vice chancellor does not talk of his success in office
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is A because to "ride the crest (of a wave)" is to enjoy a period of success and popularity.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
She was absolved by the court from the charge.
options: she was convicted for the charge
she was blamed and charged to court
her case was resolved by the court
she was declared free from the charge
questions.explanation: To be absolved of a charge is to be declared free from guilt or blame.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
The landlord is fond of throwing his weight about.
options: the landlord gives orders to people
the landlord is respected by his tenants
questions.explanation: To throw one's weight about is to behave in a bossy way, ordering people around.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
The company ought to have issued warrants for one billion shares.
options: the company has issued one billion share
the management expected the company to issue more than one billion shares
members of the company bought less than one billion shares
the company did not issue one billion shares
questions.explanation: "Ought to have issued" refers to something that should have happened but did not.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
I wouldn't have responded to his rude talk, if I were you.
options: the advice was taken by the respondent so he did not respond to the talk
the adviser put himself in the respondent's position, so he did not respond to the talk
the respondent replied to the speaker's talk, although he ought not have done so
what was advisable was that the respondent gave it back to the speaker
questions.explanation: "I wouldn't have responded" criticises a reply that was already made: he replied, though he should not have.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
He could not speak out because he had feet of clay.
questions.explanation: Feet of clay means a hidden weakness of character.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
The player wasted a golden opportunity during the penalty shoot-out.
options: The player first hit the bar
The player did not score the shot
The player scored the shot that made them win the gold cup
instead of a silver cup, they received the golden one
questions.explanation: Wasting a golden (excellent) opportunity in a shoot-out means failing to score.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
As far as Abu is concerned, Mero should be given fifty naira at the most.
options: All Abu is concerned with is that Mero should be given nothing more than fifty naira
All Abu is saying is that Mero probably deserves more than fifty naira and not less
In Abu's estimation, Mero merits not more than fifty naira
In Abu's opinion, Mero deserves fifty naira or probably more
questions.explanation: "As far as Abu is concerned" means in Abu's opinion, and "at the most" means not more than.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
As an [idiot], the boy is weak in class.
questions.explanation: An idiot is a very stupid person; the opposite is a genius.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
We were [shocked] by the news that he had lost the money.
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is B because shocked means greatly upset or surprised; disconcerted is a near-synonym, while unconcerned is the opposite.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
The principal was advised to be [flexible] on critical issues.
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is D because flexible means willing to change or adapt; the opposite is rigid.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
Bola always looks [sober].
questions.explanation: Sober means calm and serious; the opposite is excited.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
Dupe was promoted for her [efficiency].
questions.explanation: Key printed B; correct answer is C because the opposite of efficiency (competence in doing work well) is incompetence.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
The management wants to consider her [reticent] behaviour in due course.
questions.explanation: Reticent means reserved and quiet; loquacious means very talkative.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
Election processes often become [volatile].
questions.explanation: Volatile means unstable and liable to erupt; the opposite is calm.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
Oche entered the principal's office in a rather [abrasive] manner.
questions.explanation: Abrasive means harsh and rude; the opposite is gentle.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
Otokpa is a member of the [ad hoc] committee on stock acquisition.
questions.explanation: An ad hoc committee is set up informally for a particular purpose; the opposite is a formal (standing) one.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
His gift to the poor was always [infinitesimal].
questions.explanation: Infinitesimal means extremely small; the opposite is large.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
The economist concluded that several factors have been [adduced] to explain the fall in the birth rate.
questions.explanation: To adduce is to put forward as evidence; to refute is to reject or disprove.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
The presidential system is an [antidote] to some political ailments.
questions.explanation: An antidote is a remedy or solution; an obstacle stands in the way of a solution.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
Ola thought that her father was very [callous].
questions.explanation: Key printed B; correct answer is C because callous means cruelly insensitive (wicked is a synonym); the opposite is compassionate.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
He was very much respected, though he had no [temporal] power.
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is A because temporal power is worldly or secular power; its opposite is spiritual power.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
The way the workshop was organized was rather [hit-and-miss].
questions.explanation: Hit-and-miss means random and unplanned; the opposite is systematic.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
Some men will continue to cause offences until they are given [a taste of their own medicine].
questions.explanation: Giving someone a taste of their own medicine means treating them as badly as they treat others, i.e. being revenged on them.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
Okibe was rusticated for his [derogatory] remark about the principal.
questions.explanation: A derogatory remark is disrespectful and offensive, i.e. unsavoury.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
Justice is difficult to enforce because people are unwilling to accept any loss of [sovereignty].
questions.explanation: Sovereignty means supreme power or self-government, i.e. autonomy.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
There are still [virtuous] women in our society today.
questions.explanation: Virtuous means morally good, i.e. upright.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
That type of response is [typical] of a lazy teacher.
questions.explanation: Typical of means characteristic of.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
Akin is an [inveterate] gambler.
questions.explanation: An inveterate gambler has gambled for a long time and cannot be changed.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
He was too [petrified] to give the closing remarks at the conference.
questions.explanation: Petrified means extremely frightened.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
During a particular time of the day, the road [shimmers] in the heat.
questions.explanation: To shimmer is to shine with a soft wavering light.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
Every human being is [vulnerable] to communicable diseases.
questions.explanation: Vulnerable to means exposed or liable to.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
Mariam looks rather [furtive] to Shehu.
questions.explanation: Furtive means secretive and sly.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
The students' union leader delivered his speech [extempore].
questions.explanation: Extempore means without preparation, i.e. off the cuff.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
His story gave us an [inkling] of what he passed through during the strike.
questions.explanation: An inkling is a slight idea or hint.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
These policies have been [espoused] by the ruling party.
questions.explanation: Key printed D; correct answer is C because to espouse a policy is to adopt and support it.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
We must not [foreclose] reconciliation as the purpose of his trip.
questions.explanation: To foreclose a possibility is to rule it out, i.e. exclude it.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the underlined (shown in [brackets]) word or phrase.
Her findings [exploded] widely held beliefs about learning.
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is B because to explode a belief is to show that it is false, i.e. to debunk it.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
He was both a writer and a politician, but he was better ...... a singer.
questions.explanation: "As" introduces the role or capacity in which he was better.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Vacancies in the company will be notified by ...........
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is D because vacancies are made known by advertisement; "notified by publicity" is not idiomatic and "bulletin" would need an article.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
He started his career as an .......... teacher.
questions.explanation: Key printed A; correct answer is D because the correct spelling is "auxiliary", with one l.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
The driver was short of petrol, so he .......... down the hills with the engine switched off.
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is B because a vehicle moving downhill without engine power "coasts".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
His many years of success in legal practice, .... didn't come without challenges.
questions.explanation: "However" is a sentence adverb that can be inserted after the subject to signal contrast.

questions.topic: Mood, tense, aspect, number, agreement/concord, degree and question tags
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
One should be careful how ...... behaves in public, shouldn't .......?
questions.explanation: The indefinite pronoun "one" is maintained consistently, including in the tag: "shouldn't one?"

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
........... a good leader must have two characteristics.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is "first and foremost".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
We visited his house ........... three times.
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is A because "about" means approximately; "like" in this sense is colloquial and not standard.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
She was ............ the verge of tears.
questions.explanation: The fixed expression is "on the verge of".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Everyone makes mistakes occasionally, nobody is .........
questions.explanation: Infallible means incapable of making mistakes.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
The woman would not part with her .......... pot.
questions.explanation: Adjective order: opinion/condition (discarded) before colour (black) before material (earthen).

questions.topic: Mood, tense, aspect, number, agreement/concord, degree and question tags
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
We stood up when the principal came in, ..........?
questions.explanation: A positive past-tense main clause "We stood up" takes the negative tag "didn't we?"

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
This professor of ........... medicine has ......... the mystery of bird flu.
questions.explanation: Only option D spells "veterinary" correctly (with an acceptable spelling of "unraveled").

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Many workers were ............ as a result of the textile closure.
questions.explanation: Workers who lose their jobs are "laid off".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
The driver died in the .......... road accident.
questions.explanation: A fatal accident is one that causes death.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
For more productivity, the company is focusing attention on the possible ........... of available resources.
questions.explanation: To tap resources is to exploit them; "the tapping of available resources" fits the aim of productivity.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
I wanted to know his political beliefs, so I asked him what ........
questions.explanation: The reported clause refers back to the plural "beliefs" and is backshifted to the past: "what they were".

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined (shown in [brackets]).
b[oo]k
questions.explanation: "oo" in book is /ʊ/, as in cook; cool, fool and tool have /uː/.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined (shown in [brackets]).
vill[age]
questions.explanation: The "a" in village is the weak vowel /ɪ/ (/ˈvɪlɪdʒ/), as in pig.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined (shown in [brackets]).
p[a]tch
questions.explanation: "a" in patch is /æ/, as in mad.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined (shown in [brackets]).
tan[ge]rine
questions.explanation: "g" in tangerine is /dʒ/, as in danger.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined (shown in [brackets]).
[h]air
questions.explanation: The h in hair is /h/; it is silent in heir, hour and honest.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the one represented by the letter(s) underlined (shown in [brackets]).
edi[ti]on
questions.explanation: "ti" in edition is /ʃ/, as "sh" in bash; bastion has /tʃ/ or /ti/.

questions.stem:
Choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. The stressed syllables are written in capital letters.
demarcation
questions.explanation: Demarcation /ˌdiːmɑːˈkeɪʃn/ is stressed on the third syllable.

questions.stem:
Choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. The stressed syllables are written in capital letters.
impossible
questions.explanation: Impossible /ɪmˈpɒsəbl/ is stressed on the second syllable.

questions.stem:
Choose the appropriate stress pattern from the options. The stressed syllables are written in capital letters.
imperialism
questions.explanation: Key printed A; correct answer is B because imperialism /ɪmˈpɪəriəlɪzəm/ is stressed on the second syllable.

questions.stem: Choose the option that has the stress on the first syllable.
