questions.topic: Comprehension of whole or part of passage
questions.stem:
In 1951, the Government decided to start a Pottery Training Centre where new and more advanced technical methods, especially glazing, could be taught. The centre was intended to serve the whole of the defunct Northern Region, and there were several reasons for choosing Abuja. The first was the excellence of the traditional pottery made in the Emirate. Secondly, firewood is plentiful; this is a most important consideration, because in the making of glazed pottery, more firewood than clay is required. Thirdly, there are good clays, and good local sources for the raw materials needed for the glazes. Fourthly, water, which is another important raw material, is plentiful. Finally, Abuja is in a central position for the whole region and is a town where learners from many different parts can find a congenial temporary home, and where the Emir and his Council are actively interested in the project.

Nearly all the making is done by a process called throwing, so called because the lumps of clay are thrown by the potter onto a wheel-head. They are weighed out so that each pot will be roughly the same size; for example, for making pint-sized jugs, the lumps of clay will be one and a half kilogrammes. The potter sits on the saddle of the wheel and spins it by pushing a pedal with his left foot. He has a bowl of water, a loofah, a bamboo knife, a pointed stick or porcupine quill, a wooden smoothing tool which potters call a rib, and a piece of wire-like object that is used for wedging. He makes the wheel-head slightly damp, and throws the lumps into the middle. The first work is to force the lump to the centre, then he presses his thumb into the middle of the lump, using water to keep it slippery. When the bottom is of the right thickness, he begins to draw up the walls until they are of the right height. Then he shapes the belly and shoulder of the pot. He trims off any waste clay. In this way, a small and medium-sized pot can be made quickly and accurately.

(Adapted from Robert, J.M.E and Smith, L.E.M (1978) Testing English Language, AUP)

Which of the following is true according to the passage?
options: pots can be made quickly and correctly
A pot thrown on a wheel is less likely to break
the potter does not have to work hard if he uses the wheel
anyone, with almost no training can run pots on a wheel
questions.explanation: The passage ends: "a small and medium-sized pot can be made quickly and accurately."

questions.stem:
Choose the most appropriate option to fill gap 11 in the passage.

Whatever may be its wider implications, the explosion of a hydrogen bomb is, for the meteorologist, simply another atmospheric disturbance. It should therefore be classed with certain rare natural ___(11)___ such as volcanic …(12)…. But there are certain features of a man-made disturbance that require special examination. As with all events on this …(13)…, it is impossible to describe what happens in detail. However, we can be reasonably sure of the main effects, and the most impressive of these arises from …(14)…. The immediate result of the …(15)… is that the air surrounding the bomb is raised very rapidly to an enormously high …(16)…. The hot gases expand violently as great …(17)…, compressing the air around them into what is called a …(18)… or blast wave that is responsible for much of the terrible destructive power of the weapon.

Another kind of wave arises because of the weight of the air. The force of the explosion lifts the …(19)… around the bomb. The gravity waves can also resemble the ordinary …(20)… waves. Waves of this type are normally felt by human beings and they have their effect on the weather.
questions.explanation: The explosion is classed with rare natural events, i.e. occurrences.

questions.topic: Comprehension of whole or part of passage
questions.stem:
Political change and social transformation in the form of revolutions have radically altered the course of human civilization and history. Today, the world is witnessing political and social changes arising from the desire of people all over the globe for greater freedom and a voice in the way they are governed and a better standard of living. Part of these struggles and processes have become more pronounced in the Third World since the end of the East-West Cold War in the late 1980s, and in the face of the challenges being posed by the ongoing process of globalization.

While political and social changes may appear to be distinct phenomena, they are analytically inseparable. Political and social changes refer to alterations or transformations in human behaviour, norms and politico-social institutions. Such changes are often a collective response to the need to change, or a tacit recognition of a shift in the prevalent power relations in the society. Therefore, the coming to power of a new set of rulers, or the establishment of new structures and processes of governance broadly typifies socio-political changes.

It is important to note that changes can either be positive or negative. In most cases, political and social changes are caused by certain factors or reasons. These push people to collectively organize themselves to struggle for a change in the existing power relations. Another reason is to capture political power in the hope of making life better for the generality of the people. If politics is defined as who gets what, when and how, it then implies that political change refers to an alteration in the form of power and the identity of the group or class which controls and wields state power.

Which of the following is true according to the passage?
questions.explanation: The passage presents political and social change as a constant feature of history, a collective response to "the need to change", i.e. inevitable.

questions.topic: Comprehension of whole or part of passage
questions.stem:
Like all reptiles, snakes are cold-blooded, or more correctly, ectothermic - they cannot produce their own body heat; instead, they rely on the sun to heat their bodies. Because they do not rely on energy from food to generate body heat, snakes can survive on an extremely meagre diet. Some wait for months between successive meals, and a few survive by eating a large meal just once or twice a year. When they do eat, snakes swallow their prey whole rather than biting off small pieces. Many snakes have specialized jaws that enable them to swallow animals that are far larger than their own heads. Although uncommon, some snakes, such as the African rock python, have been observed eating animals as large as an antelope or a small cow.

With over two thousand five hundred species belonging to more than ten families, snakes are a large and successful group. They owe much of this success to their versatility - snakes occupy habitats ranging from underground burrows to the tops of trees, to ocean depths as great as one hundred and fifty metres. They are found on every continent except Antarctica, and although they are most abundant in tropical areas, many survive in regions marked by extreme cold. The only places without snakes are parts of the polar regions and isolated islands, such as the Republic of Ireland and New Zealand, as opposed to places in Nigeria like Plateau and Gombe States in the Northern part where there is a large population of snakes.

It can be inferred from the passage that snakes are
questions.explanation: With over 2,500 species in more than ten families living in very different habitats, snakes are a diverse (heterogeneous) group.

questions.stem:
Read the passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

There are many different approaches to conflict management, each of which may have utility in particular circumstances. A great deal of scholarship has been devoted to analyzing how and in what situations different approaches can be applied most effectively.

Conflict management approaches can be classified into two broad categories: Firstly on the basis of the level of escalation at which the particular conflict is being managed. In this sense one can distinguish between the 'peaceful' and the 'military' approaches. The trademarks of the peaceful approach are negotiation, verbal persuasion, use of inducements, denial of privileges, and subtle manipulations short of the use of physical forces, while those of the military approach relate to the use of physical coercion. The use of physical force could be by a party to the conflict or third party, to promote one side's interest, impose a settlement, or create a situation in which diplomatic negotiations can occur.

Secondly, conflict management approaches can also be classified according to the status of the participants in the bargaining process. For example, a conflict could be managed through 'negotiation', that is, direct bargaining by the parties involved in the conflict; or through 'mediation', that is with the help of a third party.

The expression third party, as used in the passage, means
questions.explanation: A third party helps the parties in conflict, as in 'mediation', i.e. a mediator.

questions.stem:
Choose the most appropriate option to fill gap 11 in the passage.

Before now, students bumped onto career by chance or through the insistence of parents. These parents had pre-conceived notions of ___(11)___ professions and gave little consideration to their children's interest, aptitude, knowledge and skills. Students' career decisions were also …(12)… by the type of secondary schools they attended. Before government take-over of schools in 1971, over 80% of elementary and secondary schools were privately owned and competition was …(13)… among these schools. Each strived to carve an …(14)… for herself by excelling in sports or academics and students often ended up in engineering, medicine, the sciences and law. Junior students tried to …(15)… the career choices of their seniors. This spirit of rivalry among mission and private schools waned with government take-over of schools.

Government's involvement in career development is beset with many problems. One such problem is the …(16)… shortage of professional career development officers. These few officers are …(17)… given the opportunity to practise. The government of Nigeria has …(18)… a guidance and counselling policy. It must be pointed out that emphasis is still at the secondary level of education. This situation …(19)… the current view that career development should start at the pre-primary level and continue till adulthood.
questions.explanation: Parents pushed children towards professions they regarded as prestigious.

questions.topic: Comprehension of words, phrases, clauses, sentences, figures of speech and idioms
questions.stem:
Read the passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

It is not difficult to make a film but it is very difficult to make a good film technically polished, suited to its audience, and telling its story clearly through the precise balance of visual and audio. Film-making is a job for professionals, the amateur always a disaster. The only reasonable exception is the local newsreel made on a shoestring and intended to serve the same purpose as a parish magazine or works news-sheet. Here the content can overcome the limitations of the maker and his temptation to try to use such a production more widely and for different audiences should be firmly resisted.

Many people have a wrong approach to film-making. Too often a film begins because someone suggests brightly, 'Why don't we make a film about this?' The idea of film is generally attractive, provided that not too much money is required. A film is then made, frequently without adequate planning or with only the sketchiest concept of how it might be used. It is right that film should be considered as a possible way of putting a story over, but the objective must be clear and the nature of the audience understood first. Then the suitability of film for the purpose must be assessed and the means of reaching the audience by film ensured. Only then is it advisable to go ahead and find the money before embarking on the complex process of getting the film made.
(Adapted from Bowman, P. and Ellis, N. (1977) Manual of Public Relations)

The expression, visual and audio, as used in the passage, refers to
questions.explanation: Visual refers to what is seen (picture) and audio to what is heard (sound).

Many people are alienated from their root nowadays.
options: They run the risk of being humiliated
They don't have a sense of belonging
They are covenant with their culture
They are forcefully ejected from their roots
questions.explanation: To be alienated from one's roots is to feel cut off from them, without a sense of belonging.

questions.stem:
Select the option that best explains the information conveyed in the sentence.
Toriola resolved to act with moderation in the office.
options: Toriola chose to always be punctual in the office
Toriola chose a strategy that was not extreme in the office
Toriola chose a hard line posture in the office
Toriola chose to act with indifference in the office
questions.explanation: Moderation means avoiding extremes.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The couple danced to the [lively] tunes at the party.
questions.explanation: Lively means full of energy; the opposite is dull ('jaunty' is a synonym).

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The government gave an [unconvincing] argument for increasing indirect tax.
questions.explanation: An unconvincing argument is hard to believe; the opposite is a believable one.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
Ado is a [dependable] apprentice.
questions.explanation: Dependable means reliable/faithful; the opposite is unfaithful.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The president complains of a [stagnant] economy.
questions.explanation: A stagnant economy shows no movement or change; a transitional one is changing.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
He came across his [one-time] friend in Lagos.
questions.explanation: A one-time friend is a former friend; the opposite is a present one.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
She [muttered] some words about the farm and walked away.
questions.explanation: To mutter is to speak in a low, unclear voice; the opposite is to shout.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
We spent a [gruesome] weekend at the hotel.
questions.explanation: Gruesome means horrible; the opposite is delightful.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
'It was a [humiliating] action', said Audu.
questions.explanation: A humiliating action brings shame; the opposite is an honourable one.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
There is [hostility] between the two communities.
questions.explanation: Hostility is enmity; its opposite is an alliance ('acrimony' and 'bitterness' are synonyms).

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
Some members of the elite in our society are [mean].
questions.explanation: Mean (unwilling to give) is the opposite of benevolent (generous); 'stingy' is a synonym.

questions.stem:
Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The hotel charged me an [exorbitant] price.
questions.explanation: An exorbitant price is unreasonably high; the opposite is a moderate (reasonable) price.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
Jumoke has a [tenacious] grip on my arm.
questions.explanation: A tenacious grip is a firm one.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
I don't like the man's [discourteous] attitude.
questions.explanation: Discourteous means rude, i.e. insolent.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The land has been promised to the tribe in [perpetuity].
questions.explanation: In perpetuity means for ever.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The population was [decimated] by an outbreak of plague.
questions.explanation: Decimated means destroyed in large numbers; obliterated is nearest.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
Aisha's mother is very [firm].
questions.explanation: A firm person is strict, i.e. stern.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The family values have to be preserved for [succeeding] generations.
questions.explanation: Succeeding generations are those that come after, i.e. future generations.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
Lekan is an [aggressive] basketball player.
questions.explanation: Key printed A; correct answer is B because an aggressive player is forceful and domineering; 'submissive' is the opposite and 'anxious' is unrelated.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The girl was [escorted] by her great aunt.
questions.explanation: To escort is to accompany.

questions.stem:
Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word or phrase in italics (shown in [brackets]).
The home team [thrashed] the visitors.
questions.explanation: To thrash a team is to defeat it heavily.

There are ...... I need to buy.

It is generally ...... that we should eat less fat and more vegetables.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Ado struck Isa with ..... blow across his shoulder.
questions.explanation: The countable noun 'blow' needs an article and an adjective: 'a mighty blow'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Tunde and Kola were not supposed to attend the party .....?
questions.explanation: A negative statement with plural 'were not' takes the positive tag 'were they?'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
The two friends agreed .... each other on the issue.
questions.explanation: Key printed B; correct answer is A because people 'agree with' each other; one 'agrees to' a proposal, not to a person.

questions.topic: Mood, tense, aspect, number, agreement/concord, degree and question tags
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Abiola is ....
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' (accustomed to) is followed by the -ing form.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
.... you do, slow down and take your time.
questions.explanation: 'Whatever you do' means no matter what you do.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
The allegation was a further source ..... embarrassment.
questions.explanation: The phrase is 'a source of'.

questions.topic: Mood, tense, aspect, number, agreement/concord, degree and question tags
questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
The man ....... he ....... complete the house.
questions.explanation: Reported speech after 'said' backshifts 'can't' to 'couldn't'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
The new manager has ..... to his staff.
questions.explanation: Adjectives come before the noun: a pleasant friendly disposition.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
My sister plays tennis with .....
questions.explanation: After a preposition the object pronoun 'him' is used.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Amina blushed and accepted ..... good grace.
questions.explanation: The idiom is 'with good grace' (willingly and politely).

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
The fruits were shared ...... the five girls.
questions.explanation: 'Among' is used for more than two people; 'between' for two.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
He .... say he ..... do it.
questions.explanation: Past 'did say' is followed by backshifted 'would'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Ali looked to the left and then ..... the right before crossing the road.
questions.explanation: Parallel with 'to the left': 'to the right'.

questions.stem:
Choose the option that best completes the gap(s).
Isa wants you to come, and ........... who is free.
questions.explanation: The object needed is 'anyone else' (no possessive).

c[li]que

[ch]apel

hew

revisionism
questions.explanation: Key printed B; correct answer is C because revisionism /rɪˈvɪʒənɪzəm/ takes its stress on the second syllable, -VI-, like 'revision'.

questions.stem:
The word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates.
Kunle saw the snake on THE TREE.

What did Kunle see on the tree?
Who saw the snake on the tree?
Where did Kunle see the snake?
questions.explanation: Stress on THE TREE answers a question about place: where?

questions.stem:
The word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates.
Laraba ran sluggishly to the CAR.
options: How did Laraba run to the car?
Who ran sluggishly to the car?
questions.explanation: Stress on CAR answers "Where did Laraba run to?".

questions.stem:
The word in capital letters has the emphatic stress. Choose the option to which the given sentence relates.
Sanada was there YESTERDAY.
questions.explanation: Stress on YESTERDAY answers a question about time: when?

questions.topic: Comprehension of words, phrases, clauses, sentences, figures of speech and idioms
questions.stem:
Read the passage carefully and answer the question that follows.

Okoli bought his five-shilling postal order, registered his pools coupon and emerged from the post office feeling as he had felt for the past ten years that the world would be kind to him. But he was not happy. While waiting in the queue, another customer had told him of a friend who had invested one thousand Naira (N1,000) and won thousands. 'One hundred Naira', he said to himself. He smiled a smile of diffidence mixed with optimism. Some passers-by noted the smile and thought it was for them, but Okoli, nicknamed 'Time up' by his friends of the Government department where he worked, did not notice. His thoughts were engaged in contemplating the vagaries of that mysterious god, football pools. He came to the bus stop and looked a little wistfully at a standing vehicle. He would have liked to go by it, his home was a mile away and the sun eagerly pricked his head, but his salary did not allow for casual expenses. He, therefore, walked home.

Okoli took off his workday clothes and changed into brown wrapper and singlet. Then he set about boiling water for his 'garri'. 'No, impossible,' he murmured to himself. To gamble on a grand scale? He unlocked a drawer set in the table and slipped out a bank account book. He opened it. His assets stood at exactly one thousand Naira (N1,000). A coincidence? But it might be an omen. In the newspaper his stars for the week had said, 'Do not be afraid to take a chance.' Why should his credit stand at exactly the figure the other customer had mentioned? But one might fail even with one thousand Naira. Supposed he failed? He had responsibilities, his father and mother struggling against a perverse land which yearly failed to yield them enough to eat. Memories of that land had haunted him, forcing him to place a barrier between himself and luxuries.
(Adapted from Fagbemi, J. A. O. et al. (1998). Integrated English Book 3. Ibadan University Press Limited)

The word omen, as used in the passage, means
questions.explanation: An omen is a sign (indication) of what will happen.

Choose the most appropriate option to fill gap 6 in the passage.

In a parliamentary democracy elections are held periodically to elect a new government. This arrangement ensures that no party has ___(6)___ of power. In a country where parliamentary democracy is practised, the country is divided into …(7)…, each returning one candidate. Long before the election day, political parties engage in all kinds of activities. These activities strengthen …(8)… harmony and also define more sharply the focus of the parties. On election day, only those persons who are duly …(9)… and own voter's cards can vote. To facilitate the voting process, polling booths are made easily accessible to the voters. At the end of the voting the …(10)… are counted. When the counting is over the party which gets more …(11)… forms the government. A candidate who fails to win a certain percentage of the votes loses his or her …(12)…. Sometimes the opposition parties accuse the government of …(13)… the election in order to retain power. Such an accusation usually generates …(14)…, destruction of lives and property. In spite of these ugly side effects of party politics, parliamentary …(15)… remains a better and more preferred way of electing a new government.
(Adapted from Addo, I. B. et al. (1978). Objective English. Lagos: Thomas Nelson (Nig) Ltd)
questions.explanation: Periodic elections ensure no party has a monopoly (exclusive control) of power.

questions.topic: Comprehension of whole or part of passage
questions.stem:
The young are not listening to their elders, and perhaps they never have. But now it happens that, with many of them, the reason may be medical. The young aren't listening because they can't hear. Just as nagging parents have long suspected, otologists (hearing specialists) now report that youngsters are going deaf as a result of blasting their eardrums with electronically amplified rock 'n' roll.

The hearing specialists used to worry about loud noise as a cause of deafness only in industrial and military situations. They knew that eight hours of daily exposure, year in and year out, to the din of the proverbial boiler factory, would eventually result in permanent hearing loss. Riveters were particularly susceptible. Then they learned that the same thing happened to aviators. After the advent of jets, the hazard applied to ground crews at airports and flight-deck personnel aboard aircraft carriers - hence the introduction of insulated, noise-absorbing plastic earmuffs.

In discotheques and rock 'n' roll joints, the trouble is not so much in the instruments themselves, or the close quarters. The blame goes to the electronic amplifiers. An old-fashioned military band, playing a march in Ramat Park, generated as much sound. But the sound was not amplified and was dissipated in the open air. A trombonist sitting in front of a tuba player might be a bit deaf for an hour or so after a concert; then his hearing returned to normal. What did it was multiple microphones and speakers, and the installation of internal microphones in such instruments as guitars and bouzoukis.

What is the result of being subjected to the din of the proverbial boiler factory for a prolong length of time?
options: A loss of hearing which will never improve
total deafness eight hours a day
hearing loss which can be corrected by medical treatment
questions.explanation: The passage says years of such exposure "would eventually result in permanent hearing loss".

questions.stem:
The preparation which a study of the humanities can provide, stems from three observations about education in our world of accelerating social and technological change. First, with the rate of change, we cannot hope to train our students for specific technologies. That kind of vocational education is obsolescent. By the time the specific training will have been completed, the world will have moved on. If our education consists of narrow training, we will not be prepared to change. Second, and paradoxically, what our students desire from their education is preparation for specific careers - business, engineering, medicine, computer programming and the like, but we will not be able to train them for a life-long career. Their confronting the depressed job market gives our students a certain anxiety, but the solution they seek in vocational training is not sufficient. Third, we sense in our students a narrowing materialism, with the good life defined in terms of material comforts. Education then means learning to do a job which will make money. I see in this definition a limiting sense of what humanities responds to these three related problems. In our changing, yet narrowing world, the teaching of the humanities finds one powerful justification - it teaches students how to think.

'Our world of accelerating social and technological change' means that
options: our world is moving too fast socially and technologically
our world is going through more rapid social and technological change
the social and technological change is more exhilarating than before
the social and technological change is accelerating our
questions.explanation: "Accelerating" change is change that is happening ever more rapidly.

questions.stem:
It has been said that there have been more scientific discoveries this century than in the rest of the world's history. Certainly the list is a long and impressive one: the aeroplane, radio, television, the domestic use of electricity in a thousand and one forms, space satellites. These have been matched by discoveries in medicine, which have perhaps been less spectacular but have nevertheless saved the lives of millions of people. Sir Alexander Fleming's development of penicillin, and the discovery of x-ray photography are just two of the things which have lessened human misery. Side by side with these discoveries, however, we must put inventions such as the atomic bomb which have increased the chances of men destroying one another.

Which of these discoveries was not mentioned in the passage?
questions.explanation: The list names the aeroplane, radio, television, electricity and space satellites, but not the railway engine.

Choose the word or group of words which correctly and most suitably fills the gap in the sentence.
Ajose and Emmanuel …….. the work yesterday
questions.explanation: "Yesterday" requires the simple past "finished".

questions.topic: Mood, tense, aspect, number, agreement/concord, degree and question tags
questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words which correctly and most suitably fills the gap in the sentence.
A large number of spectators ...... present at the football match
questions.explanation: "A large number of + plural noun" takes a plural verb: "were present".

questions.topic: Mood, tense, aspect, number, agreement/concord, degree and question tags
questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words which correctly and most suitably fills the gap in the sentence.
Take your umbrella because it ......
questions.explanation: The imperative refers to the present, so the present continuous "is raining" fits.

questions.topic: Mood, tense, aspect, number, agreement/concord, degree and question tags
questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words which correctly and most suitably fills the gap in the sentence.
When I heard the deafening sound I .......... under the bed
questions.explanation: A past time clause ("When I heard") takes the simple past "hid".

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words which correctly and most suitably fills the gap in the sentence.
Janet sat for the examination ……… she had malaria
questions.explanation: "Though" introduces the contrast: she sat the exam in spite of having malaria.

questions.topic: Mood, tense, aspect, number, agreement/concord, degree and question tags
questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words which correctly and most suitably fills the gap in the sentence.
When Ade came in, he sat on a chair and ……… for a drink
questions.explanation: The sequence of past actions takes the simple past: "sat ... and asked".

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words which correctly and most suitably fills the gap in the sentence.
Lawrence, please if you come .......... my brother in town, inform him that I am in town.
questions.explanation: To "come across" someone is to meet them by chance.

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words which correctly and most suitably fills the gap in the sentence.
Charles quickly got a match and struck it on ……… sole of my shoe
questions.explanation: The definite article is used for a specific part: "the sole of my shoe".

questions.topic: Mood, tense, aspect, number, agreement/concord, degree and question tags
questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words which correctly and most suitably fills the gap in the sentence.
Olu asked the secretary to know if anybody……… to see him
questions.explanation: Key printed C; correct answer is B because in reported speech after the past "asked", the verb is backshifted to "wanted"; "has been waiting" does not fit the past frame or "to see him".

questions.stem:
Choose the word or group of words which correctly and most suitably fills the gap in the sentence.
...... likes to be cheated
questions.explanation: The singular verb "likes" needs a singular subject: "Nobody likes to be cheated".
